source.title: Aligning Multimodal Representations through an Information Bottleneck
source.authors: Antonio Almudévar; José Miguel Hernández-Lobato; Sameer Khurana; R. Marxer; Alfonso Ortega

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures cross-modal representation alignment with CKA in controlled experiments, but examines its relationship to modality-specific information and an information-bottleneck regularizer rather than reproducing a scale-and-capability comparison.
record.gate_note: The alignment results are in Figures 5 and 6; the text describes their trends, but the plotted CKA values are not stated numerically. URR nuisance probes, downstream captioning and retrieval scores, and encoder-depth results are not rows because they do not directly report alignment. The real-world Q-Former experiments do not report a direct representation-alignment measure.
record.test_reason: The study measures CKA between an image encoder and a factors encoder trained jointly with InfoNCE. This is the modality gap inside one contrastively trained system, not convergence between independently trained models, so it is a related but different construct. It discusses the Platonic hypothesis (Anna Karenina principle, Capacity Hypothesis) and offers nuisance removal as an explanation. However, its depth and temperature results measure nuisance retention (URR), not alignment, and it never compares models by scale, seed, architecture or metric.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that contrastive losses preserve modality-specific information, which correlates with cross-modal misalignment. Encoder depth and temperature affect how much of it is removed. Their regularizer yields a more aligned space and better captioning, with a retrieval trade-off at higher β. They also report 'Information Homeostasis': with trainable temperature, the temperature drops as β rises, so nuisances are not removed as much. That result is shown for nuisance information, not for alignment directly.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce a scale-based comparison across independently trained models. It uses controlled image-and-factor encoders, CKA, and a contrastive objective with an information-bottleneck regularizer.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment is related to the omitted factor information in the controlled scenarios and is examined as β changes at fixed temperature 0.01. Other parts of the study report nuisance retention varying with architecture, depth and temperature, but do not directly measure alignment for those comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 100 factor-omission scenarios per dataset (DSprites, MPI3D, Shapes3D), estimated nuisance information in the image representation correlates negatively with CKA between jointly trained image and factor encoders (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In jointly trained contrastive multimodal encoders, retained modality-specific (nuisance) information lowers cross-modal representational alignment (modality gap).

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an information-bottleneck regularizer (β·L_M) at fixed temperature 0.01 lowers nuisance information and raises CKA relative to β=0. Higher β also costs essence information and accuracy (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicitly penalizing modality-specific information increases cross-modal alignment in contrastive training, at a cost in task-relevant information.

fits_no_version.finding: Deeper image encoders and higher InfoNCE temperatures retain less nuisance information (URR, Figs. 3–4). The authors propose this as an explanation of the Capacity Hypothesis but do not measure alignment in these comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger or deeper encoders converge because they discard more modality-specific information (proposed mechanism; alignment not measured).

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The direct alignment results are presented graphically without numerical CKA values or stated correlation coefficients. The controlled experiments use toy datasets and image/factor modalities, and do not compare models across scale or capability. No direct alignment result is reported for the real-world image-caption application.
record.rows_left_out: None of the direct alignment results were left out. Nuisance-probe scores, encoder-depth results, captioning scores and retrieval scores were not extracted as alignment rows because they do not directly measure alignment.

untested.parts: No comparison across model size, capability, or independently trained models with different architectures, objectives or data.
No alignment measured between separately trained vision and language models as they improve. The Q-Former COCO experiments report captioning and retrieval only, with no alignment measure.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
No feature or circuit universality analysis.
Only CKA is used. No variation of metric, neighbour count, or evaluation inputs for cross-model convergence.
No test of plateau, or of shared data or objectives as causes, for independently trained models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6 and V7 and labelled both 'supports'. That mislinks them. The study varies information imbalance between modalities within a jointly contrastively trained pair. It does not vary the similarity metric or the evaluation inputs used to compare independent models (V6). It does not test plateau or shared-data explanations of cross-model convergence (V7). The study's relevance to the hypothesis is conceptual: the 'minimal sufficient representation' account of why capable models might converge.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representation alignment across model sizes or capability levels, nor across independently trained models with different architectures, objectives or data.
No direct alignment measurement between vision and language models on paired images and captions as both models improve. The controlled alignment experiments use images and factor encodings.
No comparison of representations across random seeds or measurement of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No measurement of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
The study uses CKA only; it does not compare similarity metrics, vary nearest-neighbour settings, or test out-of-distribution inputs.
The controlled experiments relate alignment to modality-specific nuisance information. They do not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain it.
